title: M.N. Roy

cards.b:
Manabendra Nath Roy (1887–1954), born Narendra Nath Bhattacharya, started as a Bengal revolutionary. He travelled the world looking for arms for India's freedom.

In Mexico in 1919 he helped turn the Socialist Workers' Party into the Communist Party of Mexico, one of the first communist parties outside Russia. He then worked closely with Lenin in the Communist International.

Later he broke with Marxism and built his own philosophy, radical humanism. His journey from Marx to humanism is what UPSC asks about.

At the Second Congress of the Comintern (1920), Roy debated Lenin on the colonies.

Lenin

Communists should support the national bourgeoisie, such as Congress, against imperialism.

Roy

The colonial bourgeoisie would compromise with imperialism. Communists should build mass movements of workers and peasants instead.

Both sets of theses were adopted in amended form. In 1920 at Tashkent, Roy helped set up the émigré Communist Party of India.

Roy was expelled from the Comintern in 1929, after disagreeing with Stalin's line.

He came back to India secretly in 1930. He was arrested in July 1931 on old charges from the Cawnpore (Kanpur) Conspiracy case, sentenced to six years, and released in November 1936.

He joined Congress for a time, then broke with it. During the Second World War he backed the Allies against fascism, which isolated him from the national movement. He founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.

• Economic determinism ignores the role of ideas and of human will.
  • Making class the only unit erases the individual.
  • The dictatorship of the proletariat became the dictatorship of a party, then of one man.
  • Marx underrated the middle class, which was growing, not disappearing.
  • Ends cannot justify means. A free society cannot be built with unfree methods.

He set out these views in Beyond Communism (1947) and Reason, Romanticism and Revolution (1952–55).

His 22 theses, the "Principles of Radical Democracy", were adopted at Dehradun in December 1946. In December 1948 he dissolved his party and launched the Radical Humanist Movement.

Its starting point, in a phrase borrowed from the Greek thinker Protagoras, is that man is the measure of all things. The individual, not class, nation or party, is the centre of value.

Human beings are by nature rational and seek freedom. Freedom is the progressive removal of all barriers to the full growth of each person's potential.

Roy called his view new humanism, to separate it from older humanist traditions.

Roy distrusted political parties. He said they concentrate power and turn citizens into voters only.

He proposed organised democracy: a network of local people's committees. These would educate citizens, nominate candidates and keep representatives accountable, with rights of recall.

Power would flow from the bottom up. The state would be decentralised, and citizens politically awake. This is sometimes called partyless democracy, an idea shared with Jayaprakash Narayan.

Roy argued that political freedom needs a prior cultural and philosophical revolution, as the European Renaissance came before democracy.

Indians, he said, needed to drop fatalism and blind faith and embrace science and reason.

So a band of radical humanists should spread rational thinking through education, not seize power. This made his movement small and intellectual.

• His trust in human rationality seems too optimistic.
  • Partyless democracy was never shown to work at scale.
  • His support for the British war effort made him unpopular and cut him off from the masses.
  • His movement stayed among a small elite of thinkers.

Yet his early, sharp critique of Stalinism and his defence of individual freedom against all forms of totalitarianism look far-sighted today.

Roy was a sharp critic of Gandhi. He said Gandhism was a revivalist, backward-looking ideology. It used religion to mobilise peasants while protecting landlords and the Indian bourgeoisie.

He was also critical of nationalism itself. Nationalism, he said, puts the nation above the individual and can easily slide into fascism. This was why he backed the Allies against fascism in the war.

In India in Transition (1922), one of the first Marxist analyses of Indian society, he argued that Indian capitalists would ally with the British, so freedom would need workers and peasants.

These views explain his isolation, but also his distinct place in the syllabus as the radical humanist perspective on Indian nationalism.

Roy is a bridge between Indian Marxism and Indian liberalism.

His idea of decentralised, participatory democracy echoes in Jayaprakash Narayan's partyless democracy and his 1974 call for Total Revolution.

He also drafted a Constitution of Free India (1944), proposing a federal state with people's committees.

In the freedom movement, he stands for the Radical Humanist perspective, which the syllabus lists in the nationalism unit too.

"Discuss M.N. Roy's critique of Marxism."
"Explain the main features of Roy's radical humanism."

Structure: life in three phases (revolutionary, communist, humanist), the 1920 Lenin debate, his critique of Marx, the 22 theses, organised democracy. End with critique and link to JP Narayan.
